metadata.title: Local Ranking Problem on the BrowseGraph

extraction_notes.note: Experimental tables and figures (Kendall tau matrix, MSE table) and the intro contribution bullets restating the findings were not made nodes; empirical findings are numerical claims.
The RB/SRB/R definitions are itemize entries; spans start at the bold item label, not a sentence.
Finishing step flagged generic uses of the word 'subgraph' (e.g. the arbitrary subgraph $H$ of Growing Rings); edges were added only where the referrer-based subgraphs are meant.

sec:subgraphs.section: Subgraphs Based on Session Referrer URL

nodes.name: Local Ranking Problem
nodes.statement: This practical issue raises the problem of how well one can estimate the actual centrality value of a node by knowing only a local portion of the graph. This is known as the \textit{Local Ranking Problem} (LRP)~\cite{Chen2004}.
nodes.statement_short: Estimate a node's global centrality (e.g. PageRank) knowing only a local portion of the graph.

nodes.name: Nonexistence of efficient local ranking (Bressan-Pretto)
nodes.statement: Bressan and Pretto~\cite{Bressan2011} proved that, in the general case, an efficient local ranking algorithm does not exist, and in order to compute a {\it correct} ranking it is necessary to visit at least a number of nodes linear in the size of the input graph.
conclusions: an efficient local ranking algorithm does not exist
in order to compute a {\it correct} ranking it is necessary to visit at least a number of nodes linear in the size of the input graph

nodes.name: ReferrerGraph
nodes.statement: They introduced the concept of \textit{ReferrerGraph}, which is a \textit{BrowseGraph}\ built with sessions that are generated by the same referrer domain.
differentia: built with sessions that are generated by the same referrer domain

nodes.name: BrowseGraph
nodes.statement: The \textit{BrowseGraph}\ is a graph whose nodes are web pages, and whose edges are the browsing transitions made by the users.
differentia: whose edges are the browsing transitions made by the users
also_stated_at: Specifically, in the last years there was a surge of interest in the \textit{BrowseGraph}, a graph where the nodes are web pages and the edges represent the transitions from one page to another made by the navigation of the users.

nodes.name: Session
nodes.statement: We split the activity of a single user, taking the \textit{BCookie} as an identifier, into different sessions when either of these two conditions holds: \begin{itemize} \item {\bf Timeout:} the inactivity between two pageviews is longer than $25$ minutes. \item {\bf External URL:} if a user leaves the news platform and returns from an external domain, the current session ends even if previous visits are within the 25 minute threshold. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A user's activity (by BCookie) is split into sessions at 25-minute inactivity timeouts or on re-entry from an external domain.

nodes.name: Referrer-based subgraph
nodes.statement: For each source domain we extract a subgraph from the overall \textit{BrowseGraph}, by considering only the browsing sessions whose initial {\textit Referrer URL} matches that domain.
nodes.section: 3.2 Subgraphs Based on Session Referrer URL
differentia: considering only the browsing sessions whose initial {\textit Referrer URL} matches that domain

nodes.name: Edge weight
nodes.statement: The \textit{Weight} accounts for the number of times a user has navigated from the source page to the destination page.

nodes.name: Referrer subgraphs have dissimilar PageRank rankings
nodes.statement: Interestingly, most of the similarity values tend to be very low (<0.3), confirming the hypothesis that the user's interests are tightly related to the domain where they come from.
conclusions: most of the similarity values tend to be very low (<0.3)

nodes.name: Referrer graph identification from a random surfer trace
nodes.statement: Formally, observing the sequence of the surfer's visited nodes $\mathbf{x}=(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_s)$ and computing the probability $p_i(\mathbf{x})$ that the surfer has gone through them given that it is surfing $G_i$, we need to deduce what is $G_i$ (\emph{e.g.}, by maximum log-likelihood).
nodes.statement_short: Given the nodes visited by a surfer, infer which referrer subgraph $G_i$ it is surfing.

nodes.name: Log-likelihood gap stopping rule
nodes.statement: With this goal in mind, we sort the indices of the subgraphs $i_1,i_2,\dots$ so that $p_{i_1}(\mathbf{x})\geq p_{i_2}(\mathbf{x}) \geq \dots$ and stop as soon as the gap between $\log p_{i_1}(\mathbf{x})$ and $\log p_{i_2}(\mathbf{x})$ is large enough (\emph{e.g.}, $\log p_{i_1}(\mathbf{x})-\log p_{i_2}(\mathbf{x}) \geq \log 2$), with a maximum of $20$ steps that we consider as a representation of a long user session.
nodes.statement_short: Rank subgraphs by likelihood of the trace and stop once the top two log-likelihoods differ by at least $\log 2$ (max 20 steps).

nodes.name: Sort by likelihood
nodes.statement: we sort the indices of the subgraphs $i_1,i_2,\dots$ so that $p_{i_1}(\mathbf{x})\geq p_{i_2}(\mathbf{x}) \geq \dots$

nodes.name: Stop on log-likelihood gap
nodes.statement: stop as soon as the gap between $\log p_{i_1}(\mathbf{x})$ and $\log p_{i_2}(\mathbf{x})$ is large enough (\emph{e.g.}, $\log p_{i_1}(\mathbf{x})-\log p_{i_2}(\mathbf{x}) \geq \log 2$), with a maximum of $20$ steps that we consider as a representation of a long user session.
nodes.statement_short: Stop when the top-two log-likelihood gap reaches $\log 2$ or after 20 steps.

nodes.name: Damping factor $\alpha$
nodes.statement: As with PageRank we introduced a certain damping factor ($\alpha=0.85$); this is necessary to avoid being stuck in terminal components of the graph. Recall that $\alpha$ is the balancing parameter that determines the probability of following in the random walk, instead of teleporting.

nodes.name: Growing Rings expansion
nodes.statement: More formally, given a graph $H$ which is a subgraph of the full graph $G$, we simulate a growth sequence $H_0$, $H_1 \dots H_n$ in the following way: \begin{itemize} \item $H_0 \longleftarrow H$; \item $V_{H_{k+1}} \longleftarrow \{\Gamma_{out}(V_{H_k}) \cup V_{H_k}\}$, with $V_x$ being the set of vertices of a graph, and $\Gamma$ being the vertex neighborhood function; \item $E_{H_{k+1}} \longleftarrow \{(v_1, v_2) | v_1 \in V_{H_{k+1}} \wedge v_2 \in V_{H_{k+1}} \}$, with $E_x$ being the set of edges of a graph. \end{itemize}
input: a graph $H$ which is a subgraph of the full graph $G$
nodes.statement_short: BFS-style expansion: each ring adds the out-neighbours of the current vertex set and takes the induced subgraph.

nodes.name: Start ring
nodes.statement: $H_0 \longleftarrow H$;

nodes.name: Add out-neighbours
nodes.statement: $V_{H_{k+1}} \longleftarrow \{\Gamma_{out}(V_{H_k}) \cup V_{H_k}\}$, with $V_x$ being the set of vertices of a graph, and $\Gamma$ being the vertex neighborhood function;

nodes.name: Induced edge set
nodes.statement: $E_{H_{k+1}} \longleftarrow \{(v_1, v_2) | v_1 \in V_{H_{k+1}} \wedge v_2 \in V_{H_{k+1}} \}$, with $E_x$ being the set of edges of a graph.

nodes.name: Rings
nodes.statement: We refer to the various steps of this expansion as \textit{``rings''}, where the ring $H_0$ is the initial subgraph and subsequent rings are obtained by adding all the outgoing arcs that depart from the nodes in the current ring and end in nodes that are not in the ring.

nodes.name: Rings beyond $H_0$ are induced subgraphs
nodes.statement: Observe that, depending on how it is built, $H_0$ may not be an induced subgraph of $G$, but $H_1, \cdots, H_n$ are always induced subgraphs, by definition of the expansion algorithm.
assumptions: depending on how it is built
conclusions: $H_0$ may not be an induced subgraph of $G$

nodes.name: Referrer-based (RB) initial subgraphs
nodes.statement: \textbf{Referrer-based (RB)}. The seven browsing subgraphs built by referrer URL: Facebook, Twitter, Reddit, Homepage, Yahoo, Google and Bing;

nodes.name: Same size referrer-based (SRB) initial subgraphs
nodes.statement: \textbf{Same size referrer-based (SRB)}. To measure how much the different sizes of the graphs impact on the observed behavior, we fix a number of nodes and extract a portion of each subgraph in order to obtain exactly the same size for all networks. The selection is performed with several attempts of BFS expansion, starting from a random node in each graph, until the resulting graphs have very similar size ($\pm 9.4\%$): other ways of selecting subgraphs would end up with disconnected samples, which of course would void the purpose of this experiment. With this procedure instead, we are able to compare the graphs on equal grounds and at the same time control for the effect of size (about $3K$ nodes and $20K$ edges).
nodes.statement_short: Equal-size (~3K nodes) BFS-extracted portions of each referrer subgraph, to control for size.

nodes.name: Random (R) initial subgraphs
nodes.statement: \textbf{Random (R)}. To check whether the observed behavior has to do with the user behavior underlying the graph under examination (\textit{e.g.}, the particular structure of the graph determined by the sessions of users coming from Twitter), we take a set of seven \textit{random} graphs each of them reflecting the size of each of the referrer-based subgraphs. Thus, we can explore the behavior of browsing graphs, which preserve the size of the graphs originated by specific types of users, but that are ``artificial'' in the sense that destroy any connection with the behavior connected to a particular user class. To make sure that the size is the same, we start from a BFS exploration and we prune the last level to match exactly the size we need.
nodes.statement_short: Seven random BFS-built graphs matching the sizes of the referrer subgraphs, destroying user-class structure.

nodes.name: Fast Growing Rings convergence for RB
nodes.statement: The convergence happens relatively quickly, as the value $\tau$ approaches $1$ in the first $3$ iterations.

nodes.name: Growing Rings with selection of top-PageRank nodes
nodes.statement: More formally, considering $H_k$ as the subgraph at iteration $k$ and $V_{H_k}$ its set of nodes, we select all the external nodes in $Y = \{V_G \backslash V_{H_k}\}$, which are connected through outgoing arcs from the nodes in $V_{H_k}$. We then compute the PageRank values on the subgraph $H_k$ extended with the nodes $Y$ and obtain a ranked list of nodes. Among all the nodes in $Y$ we select the top $n\%$ with largest PageRank value, and only those ones will be added to $H_k$ in order to build $H_{k+1}$ and advance to the next iteration.

nodes.name: Prediction of Kendall's $\tau$ between local and global PageRank
nodes.statement: We address the problem of predicting the Kendall's $\tau$ between the local and the global PageRank, only considering information available on the local graph such as topological features.
nodes.statement_short: Predict the rank correlation between local and global PageRank from local structural features only.

nodes.name: Jackknife training set and structural features for $\tau$ regression
nodes.statement: Starting from the seven subgraphs in the dataset, we build a training set using the jackknife approach, by removing nodes in bulks ($1\%$, $5\%$, $10\%$, $20\%$) and computing the $\tau$ value between the full subgraph and their reduced versions. Then, for each instance in the training set we compute $62$ structural graph metrics~\cite{wasserman94social,Barrat2008} belonging to the following categories: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Size and connectivity (S)}. Statistics on the size and basic wiring properties, such as number of nodes and edges, graph density, reciprocity, number of connected components, relative size of the biggest component. \item \textbf{Assortativity (A)}. The tendency of node with a certain degree, to be linked with nodes with similar degree. We computed different combinations that take into account the in/out/full degree of the target node vs. the in/out/full degree of the nodes that are connected with it. \item \textbf{Degree (D)}. Statistics (average, median, standard deviation, \emph{etc.}) on the degree distribution of nodes. \item \textbf{Weighted degree (W)}. Same as \textbf{degree}, but considering the weight on edges, which usually referred as node strength. As the edges are the transitions made by the users during the navigation, the weight stand for the number of times the users have navigated the transition. \item \textbf{Local Pagerank (P)}. Statistics on the distribution of the PageRank values computed on the local graph. \item \textbf{Closeness centralization (C)}. Statistics on the distances (number of hops), which separate a node to the others in the graph, in the spirit of the closeness centralization~\cite{wasserman94social}. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Build a jackknife training set by removing node bulks and computing $\tau$, then compute 62 structural metrics in six categories as features.

nodes.name: Weighted degree is the most predictive feature class
nodes.statement: The most predictive feature category is the \emph{weighted degree}, which yields a performance that is better (or comparable) than the model using all the features.
conclusions: The most predictive feature category is the \emph{weighted degree}
